title: Personal Growth Over Time
keyIdea: You keep changing as you grow. Things that were hard at six are easy now, so the things that are hard now are not fixed either. To see your growth, compare yourself with past you, not with other people. Name what made each change: practice, help from someone, a new strategy, or simply growing up. A dip is part of the line, and a record of old work is better evidence than a feeling.

kid: Think of something that was hard when you were six. Maybe tying your laces, reading a chapter book, or staying calm when you were cross. Now some of those are easy. You did not notice it happening, but you changed.

That is useful to know. If hard things got easier before, the things that are hard now can get easier too. Saying “I can’t do it yet” is not just being positive. When you look back, it is simply true.

Change has causes. Usually it is practice, help from someone, or a new strategy, like writing a list so you stop forgetting. Some change is just growing up: you cannot practise being taller. Naming what helped tells you what to try next time.

Be fair to yourself. Compare yourself with you a year ago, not with the best person in the class. Expect dips: one bad week does not wipe out a year of growth. Keep old work, because a story from last year is better evidence than a feeling.
adult: The PSHE Association plan for Key Stage 2 asks pupils to know their own strengths, skills and achievements, and to cope with setbacks by re-framing unhelpful thoughts. CASEL lists a growth mindset as part of self-awareness. This lesson makes it concrete. Pupils look back at real change in themselves, instead of being told to think positively.

The key move is to judge progress against your own past, not against classmates. The second move is to name the cause. Practice, help from an adult or friend, a new strategy and simply growing up all bring change. Telling them apart shows a child what to try next. Studies of mindset find the message works best with good strategies and support, not effort alone.

Common mistakes: comparing only with the strongest child in the class, reading one dip as proof of no progress, praising effort that is not working instead of suggesting a new strategy, thinking all growth comes from effort when some is just growing up, and trusting a feeling of being bad at something over evidence such as old work.

In the lab your child puts then-and-now cards on a timeline, names the cause of four changes, sorts fixed from growth sentences, and picks fair evidence, including a line graph with a dip. Every drag has a button twin.

familyTip: Dig out something your child made or wrote a year or two ago and put it next to something recent. Ask: “What can you do now that you couldn’t then? What helped?” Share one of your own then-and-now stories too.

visual.caption: What made the change? Drag each story to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Played piano scales every day for months
A coach showed her how to hold the bat
Used a timer to stop putting off homework
Can now reach the light switch
Read aloud to his gran each night
Her dad sat with her for her first sleepover away
Started checking answers by working backwards

lab.caption: Flagship lab: put then-and-now cards on a timeline, name what caused each change, sort fixed from growth thinking, and choose fair evidence.

choices: I can’t swim a length yet.
practice.hint: Look for a sentence that leaves room to change.
practice.explain: “Yet” says it can still change. The other two say you never can.

practice.prompt: Last year Priya could juggle {a} times in a row. Now she can juggle {b} more than that. How many in a row now?
practice.hint: Start with last year and add the improvement.
practice.explain: {a} plus {b} more is {=a+b} in a row. Comparing with last year shows her growth.

practice.prompt: Leo can ride a bike now because his sister held the seat until he could balance. What made the change?
choices: He was born good at it
practice.hint: Who did something in the story?
practice.explain: His sister held the seat. That is help from someone.

practice.prompt: Sam’s first story was {a} lines long. His newest is {k} times as long. How many lines is his newest story?
practice.hint: Multiply the first length by how many times longer it is.
practice.explain: {a} lines times {k} is {=a*k} lines. Old work is real evidence of growth.

pool.prompt: What is the fairest way to see if your drawing has improved?
choices: Compare it with your drawing from last year
Compare it with the best artist in class
Ask if it is the best in the room
pool.hint: Who should you compare with to see your own change?
pool.explain: Your old drawing shows where you started. Other people started somewhere else.

pool.prompt: Jas’s reading scores this year: 20, 24, 22, 30. What is true?
pool.hint: Look at the first and last scores, then at the dip.
pool.explain: 20 to 30 is real growth. The drop to 22 was one dip, not the whole line.

pool.prompt: Rosa can reach the top shelf now and could not at six. What caused it?
pool.explain: She grew. Some change comes from growing up, not effort.

pool.prompt: Kai kept forgetting his PE kit. Now he packs it the night before. What changed?
pool.hint: Did he do the same thing more, or do it a different way?
pool.explain: Packing the night before is a new way of doing it, a strategy.

pool.prompt: Which is the strongest evidence that you have grown as a writer?
choices: Your story from Year 3 next to one from this year
A friend saying you are good
pool.hint: Which one can you actually look at and compare?
pool.explain: Two pieces of your work side by side show the change. Feelings and praise do not.

pool.prompt: Mia says, “I’m bad at maths and always will be.” What would looking back show her?
choices: Things she found hard before got easier
She is right to give up
pool.hint: Was there a time she could not add or count?
pool.explain: She once found counting hard and now does not. That is evidence the hard parts now can change too.

pool.prompt: Ben could do {a} press-ups in September. In June he can do {b}. How many more can he do?
pool.hint: Take the September number away from the June number.
pool.explain: {b} take away {a} is {=b-a} more. That is growth compared with past Ben.

pool.prompt: Ella practised spelling for {m} minutes a day for {d} days. How many minutes of practice is that?
pool.hint: Multiply minutes per day by the number of days.
pool.explain: {m} minutes times {d} days is {=m*d} minutes. Small daily practice adds up.

pool.prompt: Which question helps you most after you get better at something?
pool.hint: Which question tells you what to do next time?
pool.explain: Naming what helped (practice, help, a strategy) tells you what to use for the next hard thing.
